page: Amazon Web Services i2.4xlarge is a storage-optimized second-generation instance designed for high-throughput local storage workloads. It is powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2670 v2 processor utilizing the x86_64 architecture, delivering 16 dedicated virtual CPUs across 8 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The CPU operates at a clock speed of 2.5 GHz and features a 25 MB L3 cache. The instance is equipped with 122.0 GB of system memory, providing approximately 7.62 GB of RAM per vCPU. Storage is a key feature of this configuration, which includes 3200 GB of bundled local NVMe SSD storage. Network connectivity is supported by a baseline bandwidth of 2 Gbps, and the instance runs on the Xen hypervisor.

Benchmark data reveals moderate processing capabilities alongside specific performance bottlenecks. The Intel Xeon processor achieves average scores in multi-core stress-ng tests (14125.68) and Passmark CPU evaluations (16683.51), but exhibits poor single-core performance, as evidenced by a Geekbench single-core score of 532.0 and a poor bzip3 single-threaded decompression rate of 7.37 GB/sec. Memory performance is mixed; while read-only cached small block memory bandwidth is average at 588.91 GB/sec, large block write bandwidth is weak at 18.74 GB/sec. Similarly, database operations under Passmark score in the average tier (6516.2), but Redis SET operations are weak at 6.04 million operations per second. LLM inference speeds are also constrained, with the medium 7B model achieving only 7.2 tokens per second for text generation.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the i2.4xlarge offers high local storage density relative to its compute resources, making it a viable option for legacy storage-heavy applications that require direct-attached NVMe SSDs without the overhead of network-attached storage. However, the older CPU architecture presents a performance-per-resource tradeoff, particularly for compute-intensive or single-threaded tasks. This instance is best suited for workloads such as relational and non-relational databases, static web serving, and moderate data processing tasks that benefit from large local storage capacity and average multi-core processing, rather than modern machine learning or high-speed cryptographic operations.
